theory.title: Intertextuality, allusion and literary echoes
theory.explanation: Intertextuality describes the ways in which a text enters into a relationship with other texts. The relationship may be explicit, as in a quotation or named reference, or indirect, as in an allusion, structural parallel, adapted image or recognisable literary echo. Allusion relies on the reader noticing a connection, but recognition alone is not enough: analysis should explain what the later text does with the earlier material. It may honour, revise, challenge, parody or deliberately misremember its source. A useful interpretation distinguishes demonstrable quotation from resemblance, considers what changes when a source is recontextualised, and asks how much prior knowledge the text assumes. Intertextual links can enrich meaning without making the later work dependent on a single correct identification.
theory.tip: Identify the possible source, test the textual evidence, then explain what the new context changes.

patterns.label: Distinguish kinds of reference
patterns.pattern: A quotation reproduces wording; an allusion evokes a source indirectly; parody imitates in order to expose or criticise.
examples: The sentence quotes the source verbatim.
The scene echoes a familiar journey but reverses its outcome.

patterns.label: Explain transformation
patterns.pattern: Ask how viewpoint, genre, tone or historical setting alters the inherited material.
examples: A heroic speech is retold as a bureaucratic memo.

patterns.label: Qualify source claims
patterns.pattern: A resemblance may be meaningful without proving deliberate borrowing.
examples: The image recalls the earlier poem, although a direct influence cannot be established.

patterns.label: Consider reader knowledge
patterns.pattern: Explain what recognition adds while acknowledging that the passage can still work independently.
examples: Readers who recognise the myth perceive an additional layer of irony.

items.prompt: What is intertextuality?
options: The network of relationships a text establishes with other texts.
The use of unusually long sentences.
A text's internal chronology.
items.answer: The network of relationships a text establishes with other texts.

items.prompt: Which description best fits an allusion?
options: An indirect reference that invites recognition.
A complete summary of another work.
A list of sources at the end.
items.answer: An indirect reference that invites recognition.

items.prompt: What makes parody distinctive?
options: It imitates a style or text, often to expose or criticise it.
It always reproduces a source word for word.
It removes all humour from a text.
items.answer: It imitates a style or text, often to expose or criticise it.

items.prompt: A modern novel retells a myth from a servant's viewpoint. What has changed most clearly?
options: The perspective and ideological emphasis.
The spelling of the source.
The number of chapters in the myth.
items.answer: The perspective and ideological emphasis.

items.prompt: A similar image appears in two works. What is the most careful claim?
options: The resemblance may invite comparison, but does not alone prove borrowing.
The second author certainly copied the first.
The image has no possible significance.
items.answer: The resemblance may invite comparison, but does not alone prove borrowing.

items.prompt: Why might a writer quote a source directly?
options: To make the relationship explicit and foreground its wording.
To prevent readers from interpreting it.
To erase the source's context.
items.answer: To make the relationship explicit and foreground its wording.

items.prompt: What does recontextualisation involve?
options: Giving inherited material a new meaning in a different setting.
Repeating a passage without alteration.
Removing every reference to the past.
items.answer: Giving inherited material a new meaning in a different setting.

items.prompt: How can an allusion affect tone?
options: It can create irony by bringing two contexts into contact.
It always makes the passage solemn.
It removes ambiguity.
items.answer: It can create irony by bringing two contexts into contact.

items.prompt: What is a literary echo?
options: A recognisable but not necessarily explicit resonance with another text.
A sound effect in a theatre.
A repeated line within one paragraph only.
items.answer: A recognisable but not necessarily explicit resonance with another text.

items.prompt: Why should source identification be qualified?
options: Because resemblance and influence are not always demonstrable.
Because sources never matter.
Because all readers know every literary work.
items.answer: Because resemblance and influence are not always demonstrable.

items.prompt: Choose the most appropriately hedged claim.
options: The passage may allude to the myth, although the link is not conclusive.
The passage definitely copies the myth.
The passage must have been written before the myth.
items.answer: The passage may allude to the myth, although the link is not conclusive.

items.prompt: Complete the inversion: 'Only when the ending is reconsidered ___ the earlier reference become clear.'

content.passage:
When the council announced that the old harbour would be renamed Victory Quay, Leila began drafting a speech for the unveiling. Her grandfather had always told the story of the town's founding as a tale of brave navigators who had brought order to an empty shore. Yet the archive contained a different account: the maps showed a settlement already there, and a ship's log recorded that local pilots had guided the newcomers through the reef.

Leila's first draft opened with a sentence from the celebrated poem The First Landing. She had chosen it because every schoolchild knew the line. But in the archive she found a letter from the poet, written decades later, admitting that the poem had borrowed its central image from a much older song sung by the harbour workers. The line, once presented as a celebration of discovery, had travelled through several voices and acquired different purposes.

At the ceremony, Leila did not discard the poem. Instead, she quoted it and then read a fragment of the workers' song, explaining that the two texts did not tell identical stories. The familiar words sounded different when placed beside the neglected ones. Some listeners recognised the allusion; others simply heard a more complicated account of the town. Leila left the new name unchanged on the programme, but ended by asking whose memories a public monument chooses to preserve.

content.audioTranscript: The novel makes a quiet reference to the ancient story of a traveller who returns home after many years. It does not name the story, nor does it reproduce any of its famous lines. Instead, the protagonist encounters a series of tests that resemble the older narrative, although the order is changed and the final reunion never takes place. This literary echo encourages readers to compare the two journeys. Yet the newer work is not simply an adaptation: it questions the assumption that returning home restores a person's former identity. The reference therefore opens a dialogue between the texts while allowing the later novel to reach a different conclusion.
